description: Negative and positive externalities — private versus social costs and benefits, and why markets misallocate resources.
content_html:
When Markets Affect Bystanders

When you buy a coffee or a firm produces a batch of steel, the buyer and seller between them agree on a price that suits them both. But what about everyone else? The factory’s smoke drifts over the nearby town. The hospital treats the pollution-related lung disease that results. Those people were never part of the deal — yet they bear a real cost. This is the problem at the heart of externalities.

An externality exists whenever a transaction between a buyer and a seller has knock-on effects on people outside that transaction. The external effect can be harmful (a cost imposed on others) or beneficial (a benefit enjoyed by others). Because the market price does not capture these wider effects, resources end up being misallocated — too much of some things are produced, too little of others.

Key Fact

Social cost = Private cost + External cost. Social benefit = Private benefit + External benefit. These two formulas show that the true cost or benefit of any activity to society is always larger than what the buyer and seller alone experience.

Private Costs and Private Benefits

The private cost is what the buyer or producer actually pays. For a motorist, that is the price of petrol. For a steel mill, it is the cost of raw materials, energy and labour. The private benefit is what they personally gain — the journey made, the revenue earned.

Markets are very good at reflecting private costs and benefits. The price system automatically signals these to buyers and sellers. The problem arises when significant costs or benefits fall on third parties who have no voice in the transaction.

External Costs and External Benefits

An external cost is a harmful side-effect suffered by someone outside the market. It is sometimes called a negative externality. A car journey generates exhaust fumes that worsen air quality for pedestrians and cyclists nearby. The motorist does not pay for this harm — it falls on others without their consent and without compensation.

An external benefit is a positive side-effect enjoyed by someone outside the market. It is sometimes called a positive externality. When a household installs solar panels, neighbours and the wider community benefit from slightly cleaner local air, and the electrical grid benefits from additional supply — without those third parties having paid a penny.

A negative externality means the social cost of an activity is greater than the private cost. The market produces too much of the good because the producer only considers their own costs, not the costs dumped on society. Classic examples: air and water pollution from factories, congestion from extra cars on the road, passive smoking in a public space.

A positive externality means the social benefit of an activity is greater than the private benefit. The market produces too little of the good because the consumer only values what they personally gain, not the wider gains to society. Classic examples: education (a more skilled workforce benefits employers and the whole economy), vaccination (reducing the spread of disease protects people who did not get the jab), and public health services.

The key distinction: with a negative externality, production or consumption imposes a cost on others. With a positive externality, production or consumption confers a benefit on others. Both lead to market failure because the market price sends the wrong signal about the true social value of the activity.

Social Cost and Social Benefit

The social cost captures every cost that results from an economic activity — not just the cost to the buyer or producer, but every cost falling on third parties too. Imagine a coal-fired power station. Its private costs include coal, machinery and workers’ wages. Its external costs include the healthcare bills of people suffering pollution-related illnesses, damage to buildings from acid rain, and the long-run costs of climate change. Social cost = private cost + external cost.

The social benefit captures every benefit that results from an activity. When a firm trains its apprentices, the private benefit is a more skilled workforce for that firm. But the external benefit is that those workers may eventually move to other employers, spreading skills across the whole economy. Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit.

Key Fact

With a negative externality, social cost exceeds private cost, so the market price is too low (it omits external costs) and the good is overproduced. With a positive externality, social benefit exceeds private benefit; consumers only consider their private benefit when deciding how much to consume, so the market equilibrium quantity is below the socially optimal level and the good is underproduced. In both cases the market fails to allocate resources efficiently.

Externalities of Production and Consumption

Externalities can arise at the production stage or the consumption stage. It helps to keep them separate because the cause of the market failure is different in each case.

Negative externality of production: The act of making the good harms third parties. A chemical factory discharges waste into a river. Farmers downstream lose crops; anglers lose their catch; the local authority pays for water treatment. The firm’s private costs do not include any of this, so it produces more than is socially optimal.

Negative externality of consumption: The act of using the good harms third parties. Cigarette smokers impose healthcare costs on the NHS and harm non-smokers through second-hand smoke. The smoker’s private cost is just the price of the cigarettes — far below the social cost. So smoking is over-consumed from society’s point of view.

Positive externality of production: The act of making the good benefits third parties. A firm that plants trees to source sustainable timber also creates woodland habitats, absorbs carbon and improves local air quality for residents nearby. These benefits are external to the firm’s profit calculation.

Positive externality of consumption: The act of using the good benefits third parties. Education is the textbook example. When individuals are better educated they are more productive, pay more taxes, commit fewer crimes and contribute to innovation. The student gains (private benefit), but so does every employer, every taxpayer and society as a whole. Because the student’s private benefit is lower than the social benefit, education tends to be under-consumed if left entirely to the free market.

Three Real-World Examples in Depth

Pollution (negative externality of production): A firm burning fossil fuels to generate electricity emits carbon dioxide and particulates. Private cost = fuel + machinery + wages. External cost = increased respiratory illness, climate change impacts, and environmental damage borne by present and future generations. Because the external cost is not reflected in the electricity price, too much electricity is produced from fossil fuels compared to what is socially desirable.

Healthcare (positive externality of consumption): A person who gets a vaccination reduces their own risk of illness (private benefit) but also reduces the risk of spreading disease to others — including those who cannot be vaccinated due to medical reasons (external benefit). Because individuals only weigh up their private benefit when deciding whether to vaccinate, the market would lead to fewer vaccinations than society needs for herd immunity to work.

Education (positive externality of consumption): A student studying for a GCSE in Engineering gains skills that raise their own future wages (private benefit). But employers across the country also benefit from a larger pool of skilled workers, and society benefits from more innovation and higher productivity overall (external benefits). Left to the free market, fewer people would invest in education than is socially optimal, because learners cannot capture all the benefits their education creates for others.
exam_tip_html: Questions on externalities often use the command words “Explain” and “Analyse.” For Explain questions, always build a chain: identify the externality → state whether it is a cost or benefit to third parties → say whether social cost exceeds private cost (or social benefit exceeds private benefit) → conclude whether the good is over- or under-produced. A very common mistake is to confuse private cost with social cost — make sure you define both and show the formula Social cost = Private cost + External cost. For 6-mark Analyse questions, you must show cause-and-effect reasoning throughout: do not simply list examples. For 9-mark Evaluate questions, engage with both sides — for instance, how significant the externality is, whether the external effect is easy to measure, and whether a market solution (such as bargaining between parties) could work — then deliver a supported judgement rather than sitting on the fence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on third parties outside a market transaction. Negative externalities impose costs (e.g. pollution); positive externalities confer benefits (e.g. vaccination, education).
  • Social cost = Private cost + External cost; Social benefit = Private benefit + External benefit. Negative externalities cause overproduction; positive externalities cause underproduction — both are forms of market failure.
  • Externalities can arise from production or consumption. The market fails because the price does not signal the full social cost or benefit, so resources are misallocated.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a negative externality of production?
A) A student gaining higher earnings after completing university
B) A chemical factory releasing toxic waste into a river, damaging local fishing
C) A household benefiting from cheaper electricity after a neighbour installs solar panels
D) A worker becoming more productive after a firm pays for training
practice_questions.marks: B) A chemical factory releasing toxic waste into a river, damaging local fishing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A steel mill produces 500 tonnes of steel per week. Its private cost is £40,000 and the external cost imposed on local residents through air pollution is £12,000. Calculate the social cost of production.
Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: Social cost = Private cost + External cost = £40,000 + £12,000; 1 mark for the correct answer of £52,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why vaccination creates a positive externality.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that vaccination creates benefits for third parties (people who do not receive the vaccine but are protected because disease spread is reduced); 1 mark for developing this with a chain of reasoning (fewer people carry the disease → transmission falls → people who cannot be vaccinated, such as the immunocompromised, are safer); 1 mark for linking to market failure (individuals only weigh up their private benefit when deciding whether to vaccinate, so the market under-provides vaccination relative to the socially optimal level).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the concept of social cost and private cost, why a market left to itself is likely to overproduce a good with a negative externality of production. Use the example of a firm that manufactures low-cost fast fashion clothing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining private cost as the costs borne by the firm (materials, labour, factory overheads); 1 mark for explaining that the firm also imposes external costs (water pollution from fabric dyes, carbon emissions from transport, landfill pressure from disposable garments) on third parties who do not pay for them; 1 mark for stating the formula Social cost = Private cost + External cost and explaining that social cost therefore exceeds private cost; 1 mark for concluding that because the market price only reflects private cost, it is artificially low, so consumers demand and firms produce more fast fashion than is socially optimal — this is overproduction.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a positive externality of consumption in the market for education leads to market failure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Develops a precise chain of reasoning — individuals compare private benefit (higher wages, better career prospects) with private cost (tuition fees, time) when deciding how much education to consume; the social benefit exceeds the private benefit because employers gain a more skilled workforce, the tax base widens and society benefits from innovation; because individuals cannot capture all the benefits their education creates for others, private benefit < social benefit; the market therefore under-provides education below the socially optimal level; this is a form of market failure because resources are misallocated. Conclusion identifies the output gap clearly.

Secure: Identifies that social benefit > private benefit and links this to underproduction. Some chain of reasoning present. May lack precision on the output gap.

Developing: Identifies that education has positive effects on others but the chain linking this to market failure is incomplete or confused.

Emerging: States that education is a positive externality with limited development.

practice_questions.text:
"Negative externalities are always more important than positive externalities when explaining market failure."
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with supported judgement. Arguments for: negative externalities (e.g. pollution, congestion, smoking) impose visible, measurable costs on identifiable third parties; they are the most commonly cited reason for government intervention (taxes, regulation); the scale of damage from environmental externalities — climate change, toxic pollution — can be enormous and long-lasting; in many markets the negative externalities are well-documented, making the case for intervention clear. Arguments against: positive externalities can also cause significant market failure — a free market left to itself under-provides education and healthcare, with lasting effects on productivity, equality and public health; the case for state-funded healthcare and universal education rests entirely on the positive externality argument; in some contexts (vaccination against infectious disease) the positive externality is critical to societal welfare; measuring positive externalities is difficult but their scale is also large. Judgement: whether negative externalities are ‘more important’ depends on the market in question, the size of the divergence between private and social cost/benefit, and the time horizon. In environmental markets, negative externalities dominate; in human capital markets, positive externalities arguably matter more. A nuanced conclusion avoids an absolute claim.

Secure: Makes points on both sides and attempts a judgement. May not weigh the factors carefully.

Developing: Identifies points on both sides but judgement is undeveloped or absent.

Emerging: One-sided or largely descriptive response.

knowledge_checks.q: Which formula correctly defines social cost?
options: Social cost = Private cost + External cost
Social cost = Private cost − External cost
Social cost = Private benefit + External benefit

knowledge_checks.q: Why does a negative externality of production cause overproduction in a free market?
options: Because the market price is too high, reducing demand below the optimal level
Because producers face higher costs than consumers are willing to pay
Because the market price only reflects private cost, so it is lower than the true social cost, leading firms to produce too much
Because external benefits exceed external costs, raising the equilibrium price

knowledge_checks.q: When a good has a positive externality of consumption, social benefit is _____ than private benefit, so the market under-provides the good.
Pollution from a factory is an example of a negative _____ of production.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: A cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction
A beneficial side-effect enjoyed by third parties outside the market

flashcard_questions.a: A cost or benefit that falls on third parties not involved in a market transaction.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Social cost equal in the key formula?
What does Social benefit equal in the key formula?
Why does a negative externality cause overproduction?
flashcard_questions.a: The market price only reflects private cost, so it is too low, leading to more output than is socially optimal.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a positive externality cause underproduction?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers only consider their private benefit, which is less than the social benefit, so market demand is below the socially optimal level.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a negative externality of production.
flashcard_questions.a: A factory releasing pollution into a river, harming local residents and wildlife.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a positive externality of consumption.
flashcard_questions.a: Education — a more skilled workforce benefits employers and the wider economy, not just the student.
The cost borne directly by the producer or consumer involved in a transaction.
A harmful side-effect imposed on a third party who receives no compensation.

flashcard_questions.q: Vaccination creates a positive externality because _____.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced disease spread protects people who did not receive the vaccine.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is cigarette smoking a negative externality of consumption?
flashcard_questions.a: The smoker's private cost is just the cigarette price, but others bear healthcare costs and harm from second-hand smoke.

glossary_terms.definition: A cost or benefit that falls on third parties who are not directly involved in a market transaction.
The costs borne directly by the producer or consumer involved in a transaction, such as wages, materials and the purchase price.
The satisfaction or financial gain received directly by the consumer or producer involved in a transaction.
A cost imposed on a third party who is not involved in the transaction and receives no compensation for it.
A benefit received by a third party who is not directly involved in the transaction and does not pay for it.
The total cost to society of producing or consuming a good, equal to private cost plus external cost.
